intro: Every day you hear health claims. A drink boosts energy. A pill helps you sleep. A food lowers your risk of disease. Some claims are true, some are false, and many are somewhere in between. This unit shows how medicine sorts them out.

You will meet a navy surgeon comparing sick sailors, doctors counting cases of cholera and flu, and a Massachusetts town that let researchers study its hearts for decades. You will see how fair tests, careful counting and patient watching of whole populations built the knowledge doctors use today.

By the end, you will be able to explain how a fair trial works, tell a link from a cause, read a health headline with good questions and describe how public health protects communities. These are skills you can use for the rest of your life.
bigQuestion: How does medicine find out what is true about health, for one person and for millions?

timeline.t: James Lind compares six treatments for scurvy on HMS Salisbury
Edward Jenner uses cowpox material to protect against smallpox
John Snow maps a cholera outbreak around a London water pump
An influenza pandemic spreads around the world
The WHO is founded, the Framingham Heart Study begins, and a streptomycin trial is run
Doll and Hill publish their study linking smoking and lung cancer
A U.S. law requires new drugs to be shown effective
The CDC reports the first cases of what became known as AIDS
The Cochrane Collaboration is founded to review medical evidence
The WHO describes COVID-19 as a pandemic

words.d: a study where chance assigns people to a treatment group or a control group
the group that gets usual care or a dummy treatment, used for comparison
a dummy treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill
a trial where neither patients nor researchers measuring results know who got what
the number of people or things included in a study
a check of a study by other experts before a journal publishes it
a hidden third factor that affects both things being studied
a careful summary of all good studies on one question, found and judged by a set plan
the study of how diseases spread and affect groups of people
the number of new cases of a disease in a group during a set time
something that raises the chance of getting a disease
the conditions where people live, learn, work and age that shape their health

test.q: What was the key idea behind Lind's 1747 scurvy trial?
choices: Asking sailors which cure they liked
Comparing similar patients given different treatments
test.why: Lind compared pairs of similar sailors who got different treatments.

test.q: Why do trials assign patients by chance?
choices: To make groups alike and remove bias
To let doctors choose the best patients
To avoid using a control group
test.why: Randomization keeps choices from making the groups unequal.

choices: Feeling better after a dummy treatment
test.why: People often feel better after a placebo because of expectation, care or time.

test.q: What does a double-blind trial hide?
choices: The name of the drug company
Who got the real treatment, from patients and researchers
test.why: Neither patients nor those measuring results know who got what.

test.q: Which U.S. agency decides whether a new drug can be sold?
test.why: The FDA reviews trial data and approves drugs.

test.q: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together. What does this show?
test.why: Hot weather is a confounder that drives both.

choices: A single small study in mice
A systematic review of many good trials
test.why: Reviews of many good trials sit near the top of the hierarchy of evidence.

test.q: A risk falls from 4 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000. What is the absolute drop?
test.why: The actual chance fell by 2 in 1,000; half is the relative change.

choices: All people who have a condition at one moment
test.why: Prevalence counts everyone with a condition at a point in time.

test.q: What did John Snow's 1854 map show?
choices: Cholera deaths clustered around one water pump
test.why: Snow traced cholera deaths to the Broad Street pump.

test.q: What kind of study is the Framingham Heart Study?
test.why: It follows a chosen group of people over many years.

test.q: Which finding is most linked to Doll and Hill?
test.why: Their 1950s studies showed smoking causes lung cancer.

choices: Vaccination with surveillance and ring vaccination
The disease went away by itself
test.why: Teams found cases and vaccinated those around them until none remained.

choices: Finds people exposed to an infection so they can be checked
test.why: Tracing finds contacts early to slow spread.

test.q: Which is a social determinant of health?
test.why: Living conditions such as clean air shape health.

write.prompt: A new supplement's ad says it will make you healthier. Using at least three ideas or examples from this unit, explain what evidence you would need before believing the claim, and why.
tips: Name at least two examples from the unit, such as Lind's trial or Doll and Hill.
Use the unit's terms, like placebo, control group and confounder.
Explain the difference between a link and a cause.
Say who you would ask for advice, such as a doctor or pharmacist.
